claim: Streptomyces avermitilis, S. milbemycinicus, and S. costaricanus all produce potent nematicides or antinematodal compounds.
source: Streptomyces avermitilis, S. milbemycinicus, and S. costaricanus all produce potent nematicides or antinematodal compounds (Miller et al., 1979; Burg et al., 1979; Egerton et al., 1979; Takiguchi et al., 1980; Dicklow et al., 1993; Esnard et al., 1995) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1A showing phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Avermectin and milbemycin paralyze nematodes by irreversibly opening invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels.
source: Interestingly, these bacteria have been used to produce drugs against nematode infections, such as avermectin and milbemycin, which paralyze nematodes by irreversibly opening invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels (Cully et al., 1994; Holden-Dye and Walker, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on the mechanism of action of these compounds.

claim: Little is known about whether or how C. elegans recognizes and responds to Streptomyces in the environment.
source: Despite this usage, little is known about whether or how C. elegans recognizes and responds to Streptomyces in the environment.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: C. elegans rapidly halts backwards movement when exposed to Streptomyces strains at the tail.
source: Interestingly, animals rapidly halted backwards movement when exposed to Streptomyces strains but not Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative species used to feed worms in the laboratory, or Bacillus subtilis, a Gram-positive species found in soil and vegetation (WilpatWipat and Harwood, 1999) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C from phasmid behavioral assays.

claim: C. elegans does not rapidly halt backwards movement when exposed to E. coli or B. subtilis at the tail.
source: Interestingly, animals rapidly halted backwards movement when exposed to Streptomyces strains but not Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative species used to feed worms in the laboratory, or Bacillus subtilis, a Gram-positive species found in soil and vegetation (WilpatWipat and Harwood, 1999) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C from phasmid behavioral assays.

claim: C. elegans have the ability to recognize and specifically avoid Streptomyces.
source: These data indicate that C. elegans have the ability to recognize and specifically avoid Streptomyces.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing selective avoidance of Streptomyces but not other bacteria.

claim: The avoidance response to Streptomyces is comparable to the response to SDS.
source: The avoidance response to Streptomyces is comparable to the response to SDS (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing response magnitudes.

claim: The tail-mediated response to Streptomyces is due to a secretion product.
source: We hypothesize that the tail-mediated response to Streptomyces is due to a secretion product, as animals responded similarly to cell-free supernatants (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by experimental data showing similar responses to cell-free supernatants.

claim: C. elegans exposed to S. avermitilis, S. milbemycinicus or S. costaricanus at the head usually halt movement, avoiding Streptomyces.
source: Animals exposed to a control buffer, E. coli or B. subtilis at the head usually continued moving forward, but animals exposed to S. avermitilis, S. milbemycinicus or S. costaricanus usually halted movement, avoiding Streptomyces (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E from amphid behavioral assays.

claim: C. elegans exposed to control buffer, E. coli or B. subtilis at the head usually continue moving forward.
source: Animals exposed to a control buffer, E. coli or B. subtilis at the head usually continued moving forward, but animals exposed to S. avermitilis, S. milbemycinicus or S. costaricanus usually halted movement, avoiding Streptomyces (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E from amphid behavioral assays.

claim: C. elegans recognize Streptomyces at the head.
source: These data indicate that C. elegans also recognize Streptomyces at the head.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing avoidance at the head.

claim: C. elegans did not demonstrate avoidance in chemotaxis assays designed to test responses to volatile odorants.
source: C elegans did not demonstrate avoidance in chemotaxis assays designed to test responses to volatile odorants, suggesting that direct contact is required (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Direct contact is required for C. elegans avoidance of Streptomyces.
source: C elegans did not demonstrate avoidance in chemotaxis assays designed to test responses to volatile odorants, suggesting that direct contact is required (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of response in volatile odorant assays.

claim: The surfactant activity of SDS is not required for the avoidance response.
source: We found that the surfactant activity of SDS was not required for the avoidance response, as concentrations ten-fold below the critical micelle concentration (Rahman and Brown, 1983) were still avoided (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing avoidance at concentrations below the critical micelle concentration.

claim: Triton X-100 at its critical micelle concentration does not elicit a strong avoidance response.
source: Similarly, a surfactant (Triton X-100) at its critical micelle concentration (Tiller et al., 1984) did not elicit a strong avoidance response (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to the critical micelle concentration.

claim: SDS is unlikely to elicit a response through a non-specific detergent effect.
source: These findings indicate that SDS is unlikely to elicit a response through a non-specific detergent effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing that surfactant activity is not required.

claim: Sodium hexyl sulfate, which has a carbon chain half the length of SDS, elicits reduced chemosensation.
source: Sodium hexyl sulfate, which has a carbon chain half the length of SDS, elicited reduced chemosensation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 1-Dodecanol was not sensed by the phasmid neurons.
source: 1-Dodecanol, which has a smaller, less polar head group but the same carbon chain length, was not sensed by the phasmid neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both the tail length and the nature of the polar head group are important for the avoidance response.
source: These findings indicate that both the tail length and the nature of the polar head group are important for the response.
evidence: This is an inference from the structure-activity relationship data.

claim: The NP10 strain of Streptomyces secretes carboxylic acids.
source: Interestingly, the NP10 strain of Streptomyces (Figure 1A) secretes carboxylic acids that have these characteristics (Ilic-Tomic et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Dodecanoic acid induces a robust avoidance response in the tail.
source: Dodecanoic acid and decanoic acid induced a robust avoidance response in the tail (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Decanoic acid induces a robust avoidance response in the tail.
source: Dodecanoic acid and decanoic acid induced a robust avoidance response in the tail (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dodecanoic acid induces a robust avoidance response in the head.
source: Additionally, these two compounds induce a robust avoidance response in the head (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Decanoic acid induces a robust avoidance response in the head.
source: Additionally, these two compounds induce a robust avoidance response in the head (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sensation of dodecanoic acid and decanoic acid could contribute to the recognition and avoidance of Streptomyces bacteria by C. elegans.
source: Thus, sensation of these molecules in particular could contribute to the recognition and avoidance of Streptomyces bacteria by C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data showing avoidance of these compounds.

claim: S. avermitilis, S. costaricanus and S. milbemycinicus secrete dodecanoic acid.
source: We found that S. avermitilis, S. costaricanus and S. milbemycinicus did indeed secrete dodecanoic acid, whereas dodecanoic acid secretion from B. subtilis was not detected above background.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data described in the text and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dodecanoic acid secretion from B. subtilis was not detected above background.
source: We found that S. avermitilis, S. costaricanus and S. milbemycinicus did indeed secrete dodecanoic acid, whereas dodecanoic acid secretion from B. subtilis was not detected above background.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data described in the text and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A lower signal for decanoic acid was detected in Streptomyces secretions.
source: A lower signal for decanoic acid was also detected.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Additional cues from Streptomyces probably contribute to the C. elegans response.
source: Although additional cues from Streptomyces probably contribute to the C. elegans response, our observation of dodecanoic acid supports the hypothesis that this molecule is a cue that is produced by Streptomyces.
evidence: This is speculation based on the complexity of bacterial secretions.

claim: Dodecanoic acid is a cue that is produced by Streptomyces.
source: Although additional cues from Streptomyces probably contribute to the C. elegans response, our observation of dodecanoic acid supports the hypothesis that this molecule is a cue that is produced by Streptomyces.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing dodecanoic acid in Streptomyces secretions.

claim: There are two pairs of chemosensory neurons in the C. elegans tail that have exposed dendrites: the PHA and PHB chemosensory neurons.
source: There are two pairs of chemosensory neurons in the C. elegans tail that have exposed dendrites: the PHA and PHB chemosensory neurons (White et al., 1986; Hedgecock et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: PHA and PHB neurons mediate the rapid avoidance of SDS and other chemicals.
source: These neurons mediate the rapid avoidance of SDS and other chemicals (Hilliard et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The polymodal nociceptor ASH plays a role in chemical avoidance in the head.
source: In the head, additional neurons play roles in chemical avoidance, including the polymodal nociceptor ASH (Bargmann, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: srb-6 is expressed in the PHA and PHB neurons.
source: We performed RNA interference (RNAi) (Fraser et al., 2000; Kamath and Ahringer, 2003) to knock down the function of these genes and screened for defects in the phasmid response to dodecanoic acid. We ranked the chemoreceptor genes by the magnitude of the defect, and focused our work on the gene whose knock-down resulted in the most severe phenotype, that encoding the SRB-6 G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). srb-6 knock-down also resulted in the most severe defect among knockdowns of srb family members (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). In addition to srb-6's expression in PHA and PHB neurons in the tail, this gene is expressed in only three sets of sensory neurons in the head; srb-6 is highly expressed in the ASH and ADL neurons, and weakly expressed in the ADF neurons (Troemel et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior expression data and RNAi screening results.

claim: srb-6 is highly expressed in the ASH and ADL neurons.
source: In addition to srb-6's expression in PHA and PHB neurons in the tail, this gene is expressed in only three sets of sensory neurons in the head; srb-6 is highly expressed in the ASH and ADL neurons, and weakly expressed in the ADF neurons (Troemel et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior expression data.

claim: srb-6 is weakly expressed in the ADF neurons.
source: In addition to srb-6's expression in PHA and PHB neurons in the tail, this gene is expressed in only three sets of sensory neurons in the head; srb-6 is highly expressed in the ASH and ADL neurons, and weakly expressed in the ADF neurons (Troemel et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior expression data.

claim: srb-6 mutants are defective in the tail avoidance response to species of Streptomyces.
source: srb-6 mutants were defective in the tail (Figure 4A) and head (Figure 4B) avoidance response to species of Streptomyces and to dodecanoic acid.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: srb-6 mutants are defective in the tail avoidance response to dodecanoic acid.
source: srb-6 mutants were defective in the tail (Figure 4A) and head (Figure 4B) avoidance response to species of Streptomyces and to dodecanoic acid.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: srb-6 mutants are defective in the head avoidance response to species of Streptomyces.
source: srb-6 mutants were defective in the tail (Figure 4A) and head (Figure 4B) avoidance response to species of Streptomyces and to dodecanoic acid.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: srb-6 mutants are defective in the head avoidance response to dodecanoic acid.
source: srb-6 mutants were defective in the tail (Figure 4A) and head (Figure 4B) avoidance response to species of Streptomyces and to dodecanoic acid.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The srb-6 GPCR is required for the avoidance of both Streptomyces and the fatty acid secreted by these bacteria.
source: These data are consistent with the requirement of this GPCR in the avoidance of both Streptomyces and the fatty acid secreted by these bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutant phenotype data.

claim: Expression of srb-6 in PHA and PHB significantly restores the srb-6 mutants' ability to sense both S. avermitilis and dodecanoic acid at the tail.
source: Expression of srb-6 in PHA and PHB significantly restored the srb-6 mutants' ability to sense both S. avermitilis and dodecanoic acid at the tail (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The srb-6 GPCR probably functions in one or both of the PHA and PHB cells.
source: Taken together, the endogenous expression of srb-6 in PHA and PHB neurons, the ability of srb-6 expression in PHA and PHB to rescue srb-6 behavioral defects, and the role of PHA and PHB as the sole chemosensory neurons in the tail, indicate that the srb-6 GPCR probably functions in one or both of these cells.
evidence: This is an inference from expression, rescue, and anatomical data.

claim: Expression of srb-6 in ASH, ADL, ADF and AWA neurons significantly rescues the ability of srb-6 mutants to respond to S. avermitilis and dodecanoic acid exposure at the head.
source: Using this promoter, we found that expression in this subset of neurons significantly rescued the ability of srb-6 mutants to respond to S. avermitilis and dodecanoic acid exposure at the head (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The endogenous expression of srb-6 in ASH, ADL and ADF (and not AWA) suggests a role in one or more of these cells.
source: Although we cannot rule out a function in AWA, the endogenous expression of srb-6 in ASH, ADL and ADF (and not AWA) suggests a role in one or more of these cells.
evidence: This is an inference from expression data.

claim: Calcium influx in ASH neurons in response to dodecanoic acid is severely reduced in srb-6 mutants.
source: We found that calcium influx in response to both dodecanoic acid and S. avermitilis was severely reduced in srb-6 mutants, consistent with this GPCR having the ability to detect these stimuli.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Calcium influx in ASH neurons in response to S. avermitilis is severely reduced in srb-6 mutants.
source: We found that calcium influx in response to both dodecanoic acid and S. avermitilis was severely reduced in srb-6 mutants, consistent with this GPCR having the ability to detect these stimuli.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The srb-6 GPCR has the ability to detect dodecanoic acid and S. avermitilis.
source: We found that calcium influx in response to both dodecanoic acid and S. avermitilis was severely reduced in srb-6 mutants, consistent with this GPCR having the ability to detect these stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the calcium imaging data in mutants.

claim: The GPCR required for this avoidance response provides C. elegans with the ability to avoid potentially deadly prey.
source: The GPCR required for this avoidance response provides C. elegans with the ability to avoid potentially deadly prey.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional data showing the role of srb-6 in avoidance.

claim: The srb family of chemoreceptors is nematode-specific.
source: The srb family of chemoreceptors is nematode-specific (Troemel et al., 1995; Chen et al., 2005), consistent with a role for srb-6 in mediating nematode avoidance of Streptomyces.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on the srb family.

claim: The closest homologs of srb-6 are within the Caenhorabditis genus.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the srb-6 receptor indicates that its closest homologs are within the Caenhorabditis genus.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The next monophyletic group of srb-6 homologs contains several other species of nematodes with life cycles that include free-living soil-dwelling stages.
source: Although the sequences for most nematodes are not complete, the next monophyletic group contains several other species of nematodes with life cycles that include free-living soil-dwelling stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting possible conservation of this mechanism.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is possible conservation of the srb-6-mediated avoidance mechanism among nematodes with free-living soil-dwelling stages.
source: Although the sequences for most nematodes are not complete, the next monophyletic group contains several other species of nematodes with life cycles that include free-living soil-dwelling stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting possible conservation of this mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The bacteriovore C. elegans detects and escapes from Streptomyces species that secrete powerful toxins.
source: Our results demonstrate that the bacteriovore C. elegans detects and escapes from Streptomyces species that secrete powerful toxins.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the behavioral data.

claim: C. elegans rapidly avoids Streptomyces secretions, which include dodecanoic acid.
source: C. elegans rapidly avoids Streptomyces secretions, which include dodecanoic acid.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral and chemical findings.

claim: Dodecanoic acid has nematicidal activity.
source: Interestingly, dodecanoic acid itself has been shown to have nematicidal activity (Tarjan and Cheo, 1956; Abdel-Rahman et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2005; Dong et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The SRB-6 GPCR is essential for the rapid avoidance of Streptomyces and dodecanoic acid.
source: The SRB-6 GPCR is essential for the rapid avoidance of Streptomyces and dodecanoic acid.
evidence: This is a summary of the genetic findings showing defects in srb-6 mutants.

claim: PHA and PHB are the only two chemosensory neurons in the hermaphrodite tail.
source: PHA and PHB are the only two chemosensory neurons in the hermaphrodite tail, and they mediate a similar response to dilute SDS.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: ASH and ADL mediate similar chemical avoidance responses.
source: ASH and ADL also mediate similar chemical avoidance responses, and ADF has been shown to play a role in salt chemotaxis (Hilliard et al., 2002; Bargmann, 2006; Jang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ADF has been shown to play a role in salt chemotaxis.
source: ASH and ADL also mediate similar chemical avoidance responses, and ADF has been shown to play a role in salt chemotaxis (Hilliard et al., 2002; Bargmann, 2006; Jang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Calcium-imaging experiments directly support a role for ASH in the SRB-6-mediated avoidance response.
source: Our calcium-imaging experiments directly support a role for ASH in the SRB-6-mediated avoidance response.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The detection and escape from Streptomyces bacteria and their secretion, dodecanoic acid, are the first environmentally relevant chemosensory functions identified for the hermaphrodite phasmid circuit that inform our understanding of interactions with bacteria.
source: The detection and escape from Streptomyces bacteria and their secretion, dodecanoic acid, described here are the first environmentally relevant chemosensory functions identified for the hermaphrodite phasmid circuit that inform our understanding of interactions with bacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in the context of prior knowledge.

claim: A critical function of PHB phasmid sensory neurons in males is sensing hermaphrodite-derived mating cues.
source: Interestingly, a critical function of PHB phasmid sensory neurons in males has recently been discovered: sensing hermaphrodite-derived mating cues (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Synapses between PHBs and their normal partners in hermaphrodites are eliminated early in development in males.
source: Synapses between PHBs and their normal partners in hermaphrodites are eliminated early in development, and PHBs form male-specific circuits that regulates this distinct function (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: PHBs form male-specific circuits that regulate sensing of hermaphrodite-derived mating cues.
source: Synapses between PHBs and their normal partners in hermaphrodites are eliminated early in development, and PHBs form male-specific circuits that regulates this distinct function (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The hermaphrodite phasmid circuit regulates all chemosensation in the tail.
source: The hermaphrodite phasmid circuit regulates all chemosensation in the tail, suggesting that these sensilla may have evolved to allow the nematodes to avoid Streptomyces and other environmental threats.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The phasmid sensilla may have evolved to allow the nematodes to avoid Streptomyces and other environmental threats.
source: The hermaphrodite phasmid circuit regulates all chemosensation in the tail, suggesting that these sensilla may have evolved to allow the nematodes to avoid Streptomyces and other environmental threats.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary function based on the findings.

claim: Dodecanoic acid is secreted by crown daisy plants (Chrysanthemum coronarium L.).
source: Interestingly, dodecanoic acid is secreted by crown daisy plants (Chrysanthemum coronarium L.), which are intercropped with tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) to prevent parasitism by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita), and root-knot nematodes are repelled by 4 mM dodecanoic acid (but not by lower concentrations) (Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Crown daisy plants are intercropped with tomatoes to prevent parasitism by root-knot nematodes.
source: Interestingly, dodecanoic acid is secreted by crown daisy plants (Chrysanthemum coronarium L.), which are intercropped with tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) to prevent parasitism by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita), and root-knot nematodes are repelled by 4 mM dodecanoic acid (but not by lower concentrations) (Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Root-knot nematodes are repelled by 4 mM dodecanoic acid.
source: Interestingly, dodecanoic acid is secreted by crown daisy plants (Chrysanthemum coronarium L.), which are intercropped with tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) to prevent parasitism by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita), and root-knot nematodes are repelled by 4 mM dodecanoic acid (but not by lower concentrations) (Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Root-knot nematodes are not repelled by lower concentrations of dodecanoic acid than 4 mM.
source: Interestingly, dodecanoic acid is secreted by crown daisy plants (Chrysanthemum coronarium L.), which are intercropped with tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) to prevent parasitism by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita), and root-knot nematodes are repelled by 4 mM dodecanoic acid (but not by lower concentrations) (Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There is conservation among nematodes of the mechanism of escaping toxin-producing organisms that would otherwise be a good food source.
source: This, in addition to our phylogenetic analyses, suggests conservation among nematodes of this mechanism of escaping toxin-producing organisms that would otherwise be a good food source.
evidence: This is speculation based on phylogenetic analysis and comparative data from other nematodes.

claim: Decanoic acid elicits a strong escape response in C. elegans that is mediated by the SRB-6 GPCR.
source: In addition to the detection of dodecanoic acid, we also discovered that decanoic acid elicits a strong escape response in C. elegans that is also mediated by the SRB-6 GPCR.
evidence: Supported by behavioral and genetic data.

claim: High levels of decanoic acid are not secreted by Streptomyces.
source: However, high levels of decanoic acid are not secreted by Streptomyces.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing lower signals for decanoic acid.

claim: Decanoic acid has nematicidal properties.
source: Decanoic acid has also been shown to have nematicidal properties (Tarjan and Cheo, 1956; Abdel-Rahman et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), and decanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, and fatty acids of similar lengths are present in many plant seeds (Zhang et al., 2012), indicating that avoiding decanoic acid in the environment may also be important to nematodes, outside the context of bacterial avoidance.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Decanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, and fatty acids of similar lengths are present in many plant seeds.
source: Decanoic acid has also been shown to have nematicidal properties (Tarjan and Cheo, 1956; Abdel-Rahman et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), and decanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, and fatty acids of similar lengths are present in many plant seeds (Zhang et al., 2012), indicating that avoiding decanoic acid in the environment may also be important to nematodes, outside the context of bacterial avoidance.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Avoiding decanoic acid in the environment may be important to nematodes, outside the context of bacterial avoidance.
source: Decanoic acid has also been shown to have nematicidal properties (Tarjan and Cheo, 1956; Abdel-Rahman et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), and decanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, and fatty acids of similar lengths are present in many plant seeds (Zhang et al., 2012), indicating that avoiding decanoic acid in the environment may also be important to nematodes, outside the context of bacterial avoidance.
evidence: This is an inference from the presence of decanoic acid in plant seeds and its nematicidal properties.

claim: In the host–pathogen interaction, C. elegans is frequently attracted to pathogens initially, facilitating colonization of the host.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans is frequently attracted to pathogens initially, facilitating colonization of the host (Schulenburg et al., 2007; Meisel and Kim, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: C. elegans has evolved a mechanism to recognize and escape from the powerful defenses presented by Streptomyces.
source: In the predator–prey interaction disclosed in the present work, however, we demonstrate that C. elegans has evolved a mechanism to recognize and escape from the powerful defenses presented by Streptomyces.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The avoidance mechanism probably arose through selection pressure on GPCRs.
source: This avoidance mechanism probably arose through selection pressure on GPCRs, and by employment of reflex-like neural circuits in the head and tail sensory organs, a mechanism that may be common to other predator–prey interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: The avoidance mechanism employs reflex-like neural circuits in the head and tail sensory organs.
source: This avoidance mechanism probably arose through selection pressure on GPCRs, and by employment of reflex-like neural circuits in the head and tail sensory organs, a mechanism that may be common to other predator–prey interactions.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral and neural circuit data.

claim: The avoidance mechanism may be common to other predator–prey interactions.
source: This avoidance mechanism probably arose through selection pressure on GPCRs, and by employment of reflex-like neural circuits in the head and tail sensory organs, a mechanism that may be common to other predator–prey interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: This study deepens our understanding of the molecules, neural circuitry, and behavior used in the arms race between predators and their prey.
source: Thus, this study deepens our understanding of the molecules, neural circuitry, and behavior used in the arms race between predators and their prey.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Upon exposure to Streptomyces at their head or tail, nematodes display an escape response that is mediated by bacterially produced cues.
source: Here, we study this process using the predator Caenorhabditis elegans and the bacterial prey Streptomyces, which have evolved a powerful defense: the production of nematicides. We demonstrate that upon exposure to Streptomyces at their head or tail, nematodes display an escape response that is mediated by bacterially produced cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the abstract.

claim: Avoidance of Streptomyces requires a predicted G-protein-coupled receptor, SRB-6.
source: Avoidance requires a predicted G-protein-coupled receptor, SRB-6, which is expressed in five types of amphid and phasmid chemosensory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the genetic findings from the abstract.

claim: SRB-6 is expressed in five types of amphid and phasmid chemosensory neurons.
source: Avoidance requires a predicted G-protein-coupled receptor, SRB-6, which is expressed in five types of amphid and phasmid chemosensory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of expression data from the abstract.

claim: Species of Streptomyces secrete dodecanoic acid, which is sensed by SRB-6.
source: We establish that species of Streptomyces secrete dodecanoic acid, which is sensed by SRB-6.
evidence: This is a summary of the chemical and genetic findings from the abstract.

claim: This behavioral adaptation represents an important strategy for the nematode, which utilizes specialized sensory organs and a chemoreceptor that is tuned to recognize the bacteria.
source: This behavioral adaptation represents an important strategy for the nematode, which utilizes specialized sensory organs and a chemoreceptor that is tuned to recognize the bacteria.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings from the abstract.

claim: These findings provide a window into the molecules and organs used in the coevolutionary arms race between predator and potential prey.
source: These findings provide a window into the molecules and organs used in the coevolutionary arms race between predator and potential prey.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader significance of the findings from the abstract.
